Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

vignette:
Elena Markham was 76 when she came for treatment, a divorced White woman who had spent decades cultivating a steady public manner as a city council member. In meetings she was known for being composed, exact, and difficult to rattle. What she described in the consulting room began much earlier, in the house where she grew up, where violence between her parents was a fact everyone lived around and no one named plainly. One of the scenes that has stayed with her came from childhood when her mother was being physically assaulted in the kitchen while Elena stood nearby, small and frozen, acutely aware of the sounds of bodies striking counters, of her mother’s breathing changing, of the charged pause before the next blow. What she carries now is not a neat narrative of that night but a set of unbearable sensory and emotional fragments. She said there are times when the feeling arrives all at once—terror, helplessness, a sick certainty that something terrible is about to happen—without any picture at all. At other moments, when a memory starts to come into focus, she cuts it off internally before it can fully form, as if finishing it would be too much. And when the scene does break through, it feels more real than the rest of her life, sharper and more immediate than ordinary recollection.

Over the years, particular moments in the present acquired an almost uncanny power over her. Medical examinations were among the worst. Lying back under bright lights while someone stood over her body, explaining what they were about to do, could bring on that same overwhelming emotional surge before she had even consciously connected it to childhood. She would suddenly feel the full force of fear and bodily dread without an image, then catch herself straining not to let her mind go further. The same happened when she unexpectedly saw the offender later in life, even from a distance, or when someone made comments about family—especially casual remarks about what families should forgive, keep private, or “move on” from. In those moments the past did not feel past. It pressed forward with a vividness that made the original violence seem closer and more immediate than the room she was standing in.

Because the memories were so strange in form—overwhelming emotion without a clear picture, then flashes that felt more real than normal memory—Elena had come to experience the world as full of hidden tripwires. She could never be entirely sure what would set her off because it was not always a full remembered scene first; sometimes it was only that engulfing feeling. She learned to brace herself before doctor’s appointments, to scan waiting rooms, to tense whenever discussion turned to family history at public events or neighborhood gatherings. Even spotting the offender unexpectedly could seem to confirm that the old danger was still capable of entering the present without warning. The way the memory arrived—fragmented, half-blocked, yet intensely real—made the triggers feel less like reminders than like openings through which the original event could come roaring back.

Her work on the council gave these reactions a concrete place in daily life. Constituents often approached her after meetings to talk about housing disputes, elder care, or family crises, and seemingly ordinary comments about sons, husbands, or “keeping peace at home” could suddenly leave her feeling flooded and internally disorganized while she kept her face composed. Medical procedures had become especially difficult as aging required more of them. During even routine examinations, she would feel trapped by the position of her body and overtaken by emotion with no clear image, then work hard to push away whatever memory was gathering. Afterwards she often found herself shaken by the odd immediacy of what had almost surfaced, as though a childhood kitchen existed just behind the exam room curtain.

This pattern had persisted for so long that Elena had treated it as part of her character rather than something speakable. But recently the demands of age and public life collided. A medical examination left her so overwhelmed that she had to sit in her car afterward for nearly an hour, trying to steady herself, and later that week a remark at a council event about “family loyalty” brought back the same force of feeling. What finally brought her in was not only distress but alarm at how little control she felt she had over the boundary between then and now. She wants, at her age, to be able to enter a doctor’s office or hear a comment about family without feeling seized by something she cannot fully remember and cannot quite stop, and what frightens her most is that the memory will either break through completely or continue to ambush her for the rest of her life.
